title: The superlow basis theorem

based_on.title: Interactions of Computability and Randomness
based_on.pages: ICM2010 survey, p. 3, Theorem 2.2 and following strengthening paragraph

based_on.title: Characterizing the strongly jump-traceable sets via randomness
based_on.pages: Author-hosted 43-page version, §2.2 p. 5 and §2.8 p. 10; characterization and basis statements

summary: Strengthen the same low-basis histories to finite truth tables for the chosen path’s jump.
abstract: A low path has a halting problem computable from ordinary halting. Can its computation use a finite table whose questions are fixed before any halting answers arrive? The low-basis construction already has this stronger property. On each input its recorded-jump program makes only finitely many history updates, and each update terminates for every possible sequence of oracle answers. Listing every finite answer history therefore gives a computable bound on all its possible questions. A finite table replays the same program and computes the exact jump of every common path chosen by those histories. Thus every infinite computable binary tree, and every nonempty effectively closed binary class, has a superlow member. Superlowness is also equivalent to a computable bound on the jump’s changes of mind. Binary diagonal avoidance supplies noncomputable examples strictly below ordinary halting, while hyperimmune-freeness requires a different member when the class has no computable path.
